content: Various laboratories utilize in-house methods and reagents to perform reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assays. Although these assays are not FDA-approved, RT-PCR is commonly employed in clinical practice for the detection of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Most RT-PCR assays have a lower limit of detection ranging from 100 to 1,000 viral genome copies per milliliter. When RT-PCR assays are adequately optimized, 75% to 85% of individuals who are anti-HCV positive and more than 95% of individuals with acute or chronic hepatitis C will test positive for HCV RNA. However, some individuals infected with HCV may only intermittently test positive for HCV RNA, particularly those with acute hepatitis C or end-stage liver disease caused by hepatitis C. To reduce the likelihood of false-negative results, serum samples must be separated from cellular components within 2 to 4 hours of collection and should ideally be stored frozen at -20°C or -70°C. If shipping is required, frozen samples must be protected from thawing. Due to variability in assay performance, clinical laboratories conducting these tests must implement rigorous quality assurance and control measures, and proficiency testing is recommended. Commercially available quantitative RT-PCR assays, such as the Amplicor HCV Monitor™ and the Quantiplex™ HCV RNA Assay, are also not FDA-approved. These assays are less sensitive than qualitative RT-PCR assays, with lower detection limits of 500 viral genome copies per milliliter for the Amplicor assay and up to 200,000 genome equivalents per milliliter for the Quantiplex assay. Additionally, these assays use different standards, making direct comparisons between them impossible. Quantitative assays should not be used as the primary test to confirm or exclude HCV infection or to monitor treatment endpoints. Patients with chronic hepatitis C typically have circulating viral levels ranging from 10⁵ to 10⁷ genome copies per milliliter. While measuring HCV RNA levels may help predict the likelihood of response to antiviral therapy, sequential measurements of HCV RNA levels have not been shown to be useful in managing patients with hepatitis C. HCV is classified into at least six genotypes and over 90 subtypes. In the United States, approximately 70% of HCV-infected individuals are infected with genotype 1, with subtype 1a being more prevalent than subtype 1b. Commercial nucleic acid detection methods are available to classify HCV isolates based on genotypes and subtypes. Evidence regarding differences in clinical features, disease outcomes, or progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) among individuals with different HCV genotypes is limited. However, significant differences exist in responses to antiviral therapy based on HCV genotype. Patients infected with genotype 1 have substantially lower response rates to treatment compared to those with other genotypes, and treatment regimens may vary depending on the genotype. Therefore, genotyping is often warranted in individuals with chronic hepatitis C who are being considered for antiviral therapy. The clinical presentation of acute hepatitis C in patients seeking medical care is similar to that of other types of viral hepatitis. Serologic testing is necessary to determine the specific cause of hepatitis in individual patients. In up to 20% of patients, the onset of symptoms may precede anti-HCV seroconversion. Anti-HCV antibodies can be detected in 80% of patients within 15 weeks of exposure, in 90% or more within 5 months, and in 97% or more by 6 months after exposure.
